history.heading: Discovery
paragraphs: Antarctica is the southernmost continent and the last to be discovered. Ancient Greeks imagined a southern landmass, but the continent was first sighted in 1820 by Russian, British and American expeditions. Sealers and whalers explored its surrounding waters during the 19th century.

The Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration (around 1897–1922) brought famous expeditions. Norwegian Roald Amundsen reached the South Pole first in December 1911, while Robert Falcon Scott's British party arrived weeks later and died on the return journey. Ernest Shackleton's Endurance expedition became a legendary story of survival.

history.heading: Claims and the Antarctic Treaty
paragraphs: Seven countries made territorial claims: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom, several of which overlap. Scientific cooperation during the International Geophysical Year of 1957–58 paved the way for the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959.

The treaty reserves Antarctica for peaceful purposes and scientific research, bans military activity and nuclear testing, and freezes territorial claims. A 1991 Environmental Protocol banned mining and designated the continent a natural reserve devoted to peace and science.

culture.heading: A continent of scientists
paragraphs: Antarctica has no permanent population. Several thousand researchers and support staff live at dozens of research stations in summer, falling to around a thousand in winter. Stations range from the large US McMurdo Station to small field camps.

Research covers climate, glaciology, astronomy, biology and geology. Ice cores drilled from the ice sheet contain air bubbles that record Earth's climate over hundreds of thousands of years. Midwinter Day on 21 June is a traditional celebration at the stations.

culture.heading: Wildlife
paragraphs: While the interior is almost lifeless, the coasts and ocean are rich in life, including emperor and Adélie penguins, seals, whales and huge swarms of krill that support the food chain.

politics.heading: Governance by treaty
paragraphs: Antarctica is governed by the Antarctic Treaty System. Countries that conduct substantial research there, known as consultative parties, take decisions by consensus at annual meetings. More than 50 countries are parties to the treaty.
Territorial claims are neither recognised nor rejected under the treaty. Debates include managing growing tourism, regulating fishing in the Southern Ocean and creating marine protected areas.

economy.heading: Science, tourism and fishing
paragraphs: There is no economy in the usual sense. Mining is banned. Economic activity consists of tourism, mainly cruise ships visiting the Antarctic Peninsula, and fishing for krill and toothfish in the surrounding ocean, regulated by an international commission.
Antarctica holds about 70 percent of the world's fresh water in its ice sheet. Its melting is a key factor in future sea-level rise, which makes Antarctic science important for the whole world.
